item.query: RFC 9309 robots.txt user-agent groups allow disallow percent encoding unavailable robots.txt

action.query: RFC 9309 robots.txt user-agent groups allow disallow percent encoding unavailable robots.txt
queries: RFC 9309 robots.txt user-agent groups allow disallow percent encoding unavailable robots.txt

item.text:
Below I separate `supported fact` from `inference`, `uncertainty`, `disagreement`, and `lack of good evidence`.

**Supported Fact**

User-agent groups:
A robots.txt `group` is one or more `user-agent` lines followed by one or more rules; the group ends at the next `user-agent` line or end of file, and the last group may have no rules, which implicitly allows everything. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9309/>

A crawler uses its product token to find relevant groups. The product token must contain only letters, underscores, and hyphens, and crawlers must use case-insensitive matching to find the group that matches the product token. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9309/>

If more than one group matches the user-agent, the crawler must combine those groups’ rules into one group and then parse that combined group under the rule-processing rules in Section 2.2.2. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9309/>

If no matching group exists, crawlers must obey the group whose `user-agent` value is `*`, if such a group is present. If no group matches and there is no `*` group, or if no groups are present at all, then no rules apply. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9309/>

Allow/disallow precedence:
To decide whether a URI is allowed, a crawler must match the URI against the paths in `allow` and `disallow` rules. Matching should be case-sensitive, must start with the first octet of the path, and the most specific match must be used. RFC 9309 defines the “most specific” match as the one with the most octets. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9309/>

If an `allow` rule and a `disallow` rule are equivalent, the `allow` rule should be used. If no rule in the applicable group matches, or if the group has no rules, the URI is allowed. The `/robots.txt` URI is implicitly allowed. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9309/>

Percent encoding:
Before comparison, octets in the URI and in robots.txt paths that are outside ASCII, and octets in the reserved range defined by RFC 3986, must be percent-encoded. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9309/>

If the URI contains a percent-encoded ASCII octet, it must be decoded before comparison, unless the octet is a reserved URI character under RFC 3986 or is outside the unreserved range. The match is positive only if the rule path ends before any octet difference is encountered. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9309/>

RFC 9309 also says crawlers must support special characters such as `*` and `$`, and if crawlers need to match those characters literally in the URI, they should use percent encoding. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9309/>

Unavailable robots.txt responses:
RFC 9309 defines `Unavailable` as the case where the crawler tries to fetch `/robots.txt` and the server responds with a status indicating the resource is unavailable; in HTTP, 4xx status codes are given as the example. If the status indicates the robots.txt file is unavailable to the crawler, the crawler may access any resources on the server. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9309/>

By contrast, if robots.txt is `Unreachable` because of server or network errors, the file is considered undefined and the crawler must assume complete disallow; in HTTP, 5xx status codes are given as the example. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9309/>

**Inference**

A practical summary of RFC 9309 is: first determine the applicable user-agent group(s), merge them if multiple groups match, then resolve `allow` versus `disallow` by longest-path match, with `allow` winning ties, after doing the RFC’s required percent-encoding normalization. This is a synthesis of multiple normative statements in the RFC, not a single sentence stated verbatim there. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9309/>

**Uncertainty**

RFC 9309 says 4xx codes are an example of `Unavailable`, not an exhaustive enumeration in the text I reviewed, so I can support “4xx are included as an example,” but I would not overclaim a complete per-status-code matrix from this source alone. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9309/>

**Disagreement**

I found no disagreement in the primary source itself about these four points. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9309/>

**Lack of Good Evidence**

I do not have good evidence from RFC 9309 alone for crawler-specific behavior beyond the RFC’s requirements and examples, such as how every real crawler handles borderline user-agent matching cases or every unusual HTTP status. <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9309/>
